raw_case_text: A 14-year-old female student was treated at our hospital for PV (diagnosed by slide and antigen test) with antimalarials and discharged uneventfully after 3 days. She presented to us 2 weeks later with acute gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and bilateral visual blurring since 2 days. She denied a history of any other symptom. She had not lost consciousness and did not report any history of seizures. There was no history suggestive of any respiratory, gastrointestinal, skin, exanthema or any other infection (except PV) in 4 weeks prior to the current symptoms. On examination, she had bilateral optic neuritis, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria, and limb and truncal ataxia. Rest examination was normal. Her complete blood count, renal and hepatic functions, blood glucose, electrolytes, human immunodeficiency virus - enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, hepatitis B and C and serological test for syphilis were normal. Malaria parasites were not seen on peripheral smear examination, and antigen test for malaria was negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed T1-weighted isointense and T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense signal in bilateral cerebellar hemispheres including vermis, with minimal diffusion restriction and nongadolinium enhancement [Figure 1]. MRI of the spine was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed 65 mg/dL proteins, 10 leukocytes, 100% lymphocytes, and glucose 97 mg/dL (matching blood glucose 111 mg/dL). CSF was negative for malarial antigen test, and polymerase chain reaction for herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 and varicella-zoster virus. Other viral markers were not done due to financial constraints. CSF oligoclonal bands and serum anti-aquaporin4 antibody were negative. Visual evoked potentials showed bilaterally delayed P100. Patient was treated with Methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 5 days and began showing visual improvement by day 2 in right eye and by day 4 in left eye. Ataxia and dysarthria also improved by day 4. She was discharged on oral steroids for 6 weeks, after which follow-up examination was completely normal. Repeat MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast after 3 months showed partial resolution of previous lesions and no new lesions [Figure 2].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old female student presented with a 2-day history of acute gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, and bilateral blurred vision 2 weeks after recovering from Plasmodium vivax malaria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks after completing antimalarial treatment and being discharged after a 3-day hospitalization for slide- and antigen-confirmed Plasmodium vivax malaria, the patient developed acute onset of gait and limb ataxia, slurred speech, and bilateral visual blurring over 2 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hospitalized 2 weeks prior for confirmed Plasmodium vivax malaria; no other respiratory, gastrointestinal, or exanthematous infections in the preceding 4 weeks.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for gait/limb ataxia, dysarthria, and bilateral blurred vision. Negative for loss of consciousness, seizures, or fever.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination revealed bilateral optic neuritis, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria, and limb and truncal ataxia; remaining systemic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, renal and hepatic function tests, blood glucose (111 mg/dL), electrolytes, HIV ELISA, HBV, HCV, syphilis serology, and serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibody were all normal/negative. Visual evoked potentials (VEP) demonstrated bilaterally delayed P100 latencies.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI demonstrated T1-isointense and T2/FLAIR-hyperintense lesions in the bilateral cerebellar hemispheres and vermis with minimal diffusion restriction and no gadolinium enhancement (spine MRI normal). Lumbar puncture CSF showed protein 65 mg/dL, 10 leukocytes/uL (100% lymphocytes), glucose 97 mg/dL, negative oligoclonal bands, negative malarial antigen, and negative HSV-1/2 and VZV PCR.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Post-malarial acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) presenting with bilateral optic neuritis and pancerebellar ataxia following Plasmodium vivax malaria. Active malaria at representation was excluded by negative peripheral blood smear, blood malaria antigen test, and CSF malaria antigen test. Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 5 days followed by a 6-week oral steroid taper; visual acuity improved by days 2-4, ataxia and dysarthria improved by day 4, neurological exam was completely normal at 6 weeks, and 3-month repeat brain MRI showed partial lesion resolution with no new lesions.
